fetched_contents.text: Learner-Generated Drawing Holds Potential for both Learning and Assessment – UAF Center for Teaching and Learning This teaching tip has two main components. The first is a brief survey of recent peer reviewed journal articles on learner-generated drawing as the basis for learning activities and assessments. The second is reflections and conversational highlights from University of Alaska Fairbanks’ Don Larson and Shayla Sackinger, who share faculty and student perspectives on creative exercises in general and illustration activities in particular. In order to avoid imprecise vocabulary use, the phrase ‘learner-generated drawings’ will use the working definition from van Meter and Garner’s 2005 The promise and practice of learner-generated drawing. These authors distinguish between clearly labeled drawings that illustrate a complex structure or spatial representation from works that incorporate more artistic styles such as those found in impressionistic, cubist, or surreal styles. Further, the authors define learner-generated drawings as having three qualities: They are created intentionally to meet an educational goal; they are meant to represent subjects accurately; and the learner is responsible for the development and final appearance. This subject began to generate research articles in the 1970s, but the results were mixed, and the field became less popular until about 2005 when researchers focused on a more narrowly defined idea of what a learner-generated drawing was, and the quality upon which it was generated. Researchers did start noticing that there was a strong correlation between accurately produced illustrations by students and later memory retention and performance on more typical assessments. Although the question of why this occurs was partially addressed by earlier efforts, the authors of The drawing effect: Evidence for reliable and robust memory benefits in free recall conducted careful research with a variety of factors on student drawing as a learning activity. They concluded that “the process of drawing a verbal item engages at least four components.” Their argument was that in order to transfer something from spoken or written word into imagery, the student must first engage in an elaborative effort, representing physical characteristics of a subject visually. In doing this the student must employ hand and eye movements to draw something. The result is that an image is created, not only on paper, but in the student’s mind [2]. Takeaways * Learner-generated drawing is similar to summarization, self-questioning or prior knowledge activation. The behavior of producing a drawing is believed to direct cognitive processes responsible for task performance [1]. * Learners may need prompts and examples, especially if they have little experience with creating illustrations * Student created illustrations can optionally be shared with the public via work portfolios, such as the one associated with UAF’s Human Anatomy and Physiology course at: humanap.community.uaf.edu. This practice can benefit students in future semesters. Do all drawing efforts have equal benefits for memory and later assessment performance? Not exactly. Although asking students to sketch things during a lecture, or during periodic breaks after reading text does engage various cognitive and metacognitive processes which are beneficial to learning, these effects begin to diminish when the drawing activity itself becomes a “highly demanding cognitive task” [3]. In other words, if a student needs to concentrate to a large degree on the process of drawing itself and perhaps doesn’t have much in the way of what we’d consider artistic ability, the positive effects of memory retention and comprehension are somewhat diminished. The good news is that the same study offered advice to provide all students with support to lessen the reluctance to generate a drawing by providing a drawing prompt. The authors urge that prompts be provided to students so that they can minimize their need to focus on the mechanics of drawing. Such prompts could be examples of other helpful sketches or the beginning stages of a completed drawing. fetched_contents.text: Scaffolding Writing to Support Student Development Scaffolding Writing to Support Student Development Resources for Teaching Writing Course & Assignment Design Feedback & Assessment Teaching Online and with AI Scaffolding Writing to Support Student Development Experts tend to complete writing tasks more quickly than novices by combining or skipping steps due to years of practice and mastery. Our students often come to us as novices who are still learning what the initial steps themselves are. Complex writing tasks (like bigger projects or discipline-specific writing tasks) should thus be broken into smaller chunks that students learn in segments as they expand their skills over time. What is scaffolding? Scaffolding is understood in educational contexts as a teaching method where the instructor gradually removes support as students learn and become more competent in a specific skill. Put another way, the instructor provides guidance and breaks down complicated pieces into smaller, digestible “chunks” that are carefully organized as students progress through an assignment, unit, or course. In writing assignments, scaffolding often appears as breaking down a larger project into smaller component parts, or learning more set of skills related to writing before asking students to produce writing in a specific genre. This resource outlines some strategies and recommendations for how to scaffold writing for learning across your assignments and your courses. Before you begin designing the assignment, ask: * What overall course learning outcomes does this assignment meet? * What criteria will you use to evaluate the end product? * What skills would students need to develop to meet those criteria? * What steps might experts follow in completing this writing task? Recommendations for Scaffolding Writing for Learning 1. Break your writing assignment into smaller pieces due throughout the unit or semester. Studies show that students can feel overwhelmed thinking about a large, imposing writing assignment yet find it more manageable to complete parts along the way. Consider breaking up your major writing assignment into separate pieces that are turned in throughout the project, such as a literature review, and then an analysis, etc. Students can work on these throughout the semester and then combine it into a longer, fuller project at the end, after already receiving some feedback and time to work on it. 2. Incorporate both low-stakes and high-stakes writing activities in your course. Not all writing assignments and activities need to be large, extensive projects. To support student learning, build in both low stakes and high stakes writing assignments to encourage students to practice and develop their knowledge and skills as they work towards the larger assignment. Generally, low stakes writing (like free writes, a quick reflective paragraph, peer response, etc.) is not evaluated for grammar, polish, fully developed thoughts, or correctness. In these types of assignments, students can feel free to explore ideas, make mistakes, and focus on their ideas or the task. The goal here is making visible their thoughts and ideas. You can grade this as credit/no credit, check/check plus/check minus, or a few points. It’s not always necessary for you to review this type of writing like you might with more formal, higher-stakes writing. 3. Calculate how long students need to learn a specific writing task when determining deadlines and mid-markers. New writing tasks can take longer for novices to learn as they work to learn all of the component parts (see How People Learn, 2000). Writing a literature review, for example, includes learning to read academic articles critically, how to take helpful notes, and other component skills. Think through when your students’ final assignments are due and build in check-in points throughout the unit to guide them toward that final outcome. Refer to our backwards design worksheet to think through all the skills and tasks necessary for completing the larger writing assignment. 4. Evaluate where students often get stuck or confused. Research on threshold concepts indicates that determining where students get “stuck” in the learning process can be a helpful indicator of where you can intervene to provide more structured and sequenced support. For example, if students often get stuck when writing a methods section, you can take twenty minutes or so to discuss this with the entire class, perhaps incorporating some low-stakes activities as mentioned above. Ask students if they’ve written a methods section before (and where), and have them describe it. Provide a few samples (3-5) of method sections written previously in your class and ask students to evaluate them, writing out what they are doing (and not doing), given your evaluation criteria. 5. Insert frequent opportunities for students to receive feedback on their writing and ideas. fetched_contents.text: ICLS2012 Volume 2: Short Papers Using the learner-generated drawing strategy: How much instructional support is useful? Annett Schmeck (nee Schwamborn), Luisa Friedrich, Maria Opfermann, & Detlev Leutner, Instructional Psychology, Duisburg-Essen University, 45117 Essen E-mail: annett.schmeck@uni-due.de, luisa.friedrich@uni-due.de, maria.opfermann@uni-due.de, detlev.leutner@uni-due.de Learner-generated drawing is a learning strategy which is used to improve students' text comprehension. Research has shown that benefits of the learner-generated drawing strategy strongly depend on drawing-accuracy and that students need instructional support to draw accurate drawings. However, less is known about how much support is needed. Thus, in the present study, one hundred and two 9th graders read a science text and were instructed to generate drawings during reading with varying degrees of instructional support. Results show that students who learnt with a toolbar showing all the relevant elements for drawing showed higher drawing-accuracy scores associated with less learning time than students who learnt with pre-drawn drawing backgrounds or those who learnt without any support during drawing. Objective and Theoretical Framework Students reading complex and difficult scientific texts do often have problems with the cognitively highly demanding processes of text comprehension. Based on models of self-regulated learning (e.g., Boekaerts, 1999; Weinstein & Mayer, 1986; Zimmerman, 2001) the so-called learner-generated drawing strategy is one possible way to foster students' text comprehension (Alesandrini, 1984; Schwamborn, Mayer, Thillmann, Leopold, & Leutner, 2010; van Meter & Garner, 2005). In doing so, students' are instructed to read a text and to generate drawings by themselves that reflect the important ideas of the text. According to van Meter and Garner (2005) this generation process causes students to engage in cognitive and metacognitive processes which foster deep- level understanding of the to-be-learned information. The integration of the internal verbal and pictorial representations into a coherent mental model, for example, is induced (Mayer, 2009). Additionally, metacognitive processes such as self-monitoring and self-regulation are induced. Thus, drawing a picture to a text is a productive learning activity that encourages generative processing and thus fosters deep level understanding (de Jong, 2005; Kirschner, Sweller, & Clark, 2006; Mayer, 2003, 2004; Schwamborn et al., 2010). However, instructing students to generate drawings to a text does not automatically guarantee deep level understanding. Problems concerning the product of drawing can occur, like a low quality of the students' self-generated drawings (Leopold, 2009; van Meter, 2001; van Meter, Aleksic, Schwartz, & Garner, 2006). A low quality of the self-generated drawing means that the drawing does not accurately reflect all important ideas and causal relations that are described in the text which are necessary for deep-level understanding. Thus, benefits of the learner-generated drawing strategy depend on the quality respectively the accuracy of students' self-generated drawings during reading - which is the so-called prognostic drawing effect (Schwamborn et al., 2010). Accordingly, research on the learner-generated drawing strategy showed that the accuracy of students' self-generated drawings respectively the benefits of the strategy depend on scaffolding students to use the strategy appropriately. That is, positive effects of the strategy on text comprehension depend on the instructional support mediated by the accuracy of the learner-generated drawings (e.g. Schwamborn et al., 2010). In studies of Leutner, Leopold, and Sumfleth (2009) and Alesandrini (1981), for example, students' did not benefit from using the pure, unsupported learner-generated drawing strategy. Lesgold, Levin, Shimron, and Guttman (1975), van Meter et al. (2001, 2006), and Schwamborn et al. (2010), however, instructionally supported the drawing process in their studies and found benefits of the drawing strategy. Van Meter et al. (2001, 2006), for example, supported students with illustrations and prompting questions after the drawing process. Lesgold et al. (1975) supported students during the generation process by giving them cut-out figures. Accordingly, Schwamborn et al. (2010) implemented a drawing prompt to instructionally support students during the drawing process and thus to increase the accuracy of the generated drawings. The drawing prompt included (a) a toolbar showing (and labeling) all the relevant elements for drawing and (b) partly pre-drawn backgrounds for students' drawings (see Figure 1). The authors found a significant positive effect of the learner-generated drawing strategy on text comprehension. Thereby high-accuracy drawers outperformed low-accuracy drawers. In sum, research on the learner-generated drawing strategy has shown that benefits of the strategy strongly depend on the accuracy of students' drawing during reading the text. That is, the accuracy of learners' drawings during learning can predict the quality of their text comprehension. Additonally, results of Schwamborn et al. Learner-generated drawings support planning and organizational thinking by helping students externalize and structure complex information before writing. The evidence here points to drawing as a tool that can map out sequences, transitions, and logical flow, and that it can support outlining, drafting, and revision decisions, though the provided material is more general than highly specific to writing tasks.

On mapping sequences and logical flow, the visual-planning evidence emphasizes that sketching helps people “structure things” and “clarify what I'm doing” [N2-R1]. That is consistent with the idea that drawing can serve as a spatial and visual scaffold for organizing steps or relationships, even if the excerpts do not directly describe narrative or argument structure. The writing-cooperative excerpt also notes that some people “need colors, cues, shapes, etc.” on their planning page, while others want a hierarchy structure of ideas, which suggests that drawing can accommodate both visual and hierarchical ways of representing the order of a task [N2-R4]. This aligns with the broader claim that drawing supports planning by making implicit structure visible.

For outlining, drafting, and revision decisions, the evidence is more indirect but still supportive. The YouTube example on creating an outline for persuasive writing shows that outlining is used to plan writing and that it is a common instructional practice [N2-R2]. The outline-and-plan guide similarly defines an outline as a structured document listing the main parts of a writing product, reinforcing the role of outlining in organizing a writing task [N2-R3]. The “adjusting organization for different types of writers” excerpt notes that some people prefer cues, shapes, or colors, which again points to drawing as a flexible outlining tool [N2-R4]. The writing-process excerpt also frames planning as part of the writing cycle, including generating ideas, organizing, outlining, and revising [N3-R2]. While this is not directly about drawing, it establishes the instructional context in which drawing can support outlining and later revision.

The evidence linking drawing to better planning or more coherent writing products is thinner in the provided material, but still suggestive. The UAF Center for Teaching and Learning survey notes that learner-generated drawing can be used as a basis for learning activities and assessments, and that it is “similar to summarization, self-questioning, or prior knowledge activation” [N4-F1]. This suggests that drawing can support the cognitive processes needed for coherent planning. The same source also says that student-created illustrations can be used formatively to assess comprehension shortcomings, which implies that drawing can help identify gaps in understanding that may otherwise disrupt planning [N4-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct study showing improved planning or writing quality in the provided excerpts, so that conclusion should be stated cautiously.

Overall, the evidence supports the idea that drawing helps students map out sequences and transitions, supports outlining and revision decisions, and can improve planning by making structure visible and by enabling formative assessment of comprehension. The strongest claims are that drawing can help structure thinking and that some learners benefit from visual cues and prompts [N2-R1][N2-R4][N4-F1]. The evidence for improved writing coherence is plausible but not directly quantified here [N2-R2][N2-R3][N3-R2].

The contextual factors and limitations of using learner-generated drawings are clear in the provided evidence: some learners and tasks benefit more, but drawing can fail to improve outcomes or even interfere when support is inadequate, task design is poor, or feedback is not aligned with the goal.

On which learner populations or writing tasks benefit most, the evidence suggests that visual learners, students with little experience, and those needing scaffolding benefit most. The UAF survey notes that learner-generated drawing is similar to summarization, self-questioning, or prior knowledge activation, and that learners may need prompts and examples, especially if they have little experience with creating illustrations [N4-F1]. The scaffolding evidence also emphasizes that novices often need support, and that complex writing tasks should be broken into smaller chunks as students expand their skills [N5-F3]. This implies that learners who are novices, visual learners, or those who struggle with organizing ideas are the ones who benefit most from drawing. The ISLS paper on learner-generated drawing further states that benefits depend on drawing accuracy and that students need instructional support to draw accurately, with high-accuracy drawers outperforming low-accuracy drawers [N6-F2]. So the most beneficial population appears to be students who can produce accurate illustrations, which in turn depends on prior knowledge and instructional support.

On when drawing may not improve outcomes or could even interfere, the evidence is more cautionary. The ISLS paper says that benefits strongly depend on drawing accuracy and that unsupported drawing does not automatically guarantee deep understanding [N6-F2]. It also notes that students can fail to benefit from the pure, unsupported learner-generated drawing strategy [N6-F2]. The UAF survey similarly warns that not all drawing efforts have equal benefits for memory and later assessment performance, and that effects diminish when the drawing activity becomes a “highly demanding cognitive task” [N4-F1]. In other words, if students must focus too much on the mechanics of drawing rather than the content of the task, the positive effects can weaken. The same survey also says that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience [N4-F1], which implies that unstructured drawing can be a barrier for some students. Taken together, the evidence suggests that drawing can interfere when students lack support, when the task becomes too visually demanding, or when students are asked to draw without clear guidance [N4-F1][N6-F2].

On how task design, instruction, and feedback affect effectiveness, the evidence is strong. The ISLS paper explicitly says benefits depend on the amount of support required and that students need instructional support during the drawing process, including prompts and partly pre-drawn backgrounds [N6-F2]. The scaffolding evidence recommends breaking writing into smaller parts, using low- and high-stakes writing activities, providing feedback, and allowing revision [N5-F3]. It also emphasizes that instruction should gradually remove support as students become competent [N5-F3]. The UAF survey adds that prompts and examples can reduce reluctance to draw, and that illustrations can be used formatively to assess comprehension [N4-F1]. These points indicate that effective implementation requires clear prompts, examples, feedback, and structured task design. The ISLS paper also notes that the amount of support needed is still an open question, and that the study only tested a drawing prompt but did not conduct a treatment-check of its effectiveness [N6-F2]. That means the evidence supports task design and instruction as crucial, but also acknowledges that the optimal amount of support is not fully settled [N6-F2].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that learner-generated drawings are most helpful for novices, visual learners, and students needing scaffolding; less helpful when students lack support or when the task becomes too cognitively demanding; and most effective when task design includes prompts, examples, feedback, and structured support [N4-F1][N5-F3][N6-F2]. The main limitations are insufficient support, unclear prompts, and a mismatch between drawing demands and the learner’s experience or cognitive load [N4-F1][N6-F2].

Practical implementation and classroom use of learner-generated drawing depend on well-designed activities, step-by-step integration into writing instruction, and attention to resource needs and barriers.

On classroom activities or prompts that work best for learners, the evidence suggests prompts, examples, and low-stakes practice. The UAF survey notes that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience with creating illustrations [N4-F1]. The ISLS paper also emphasizes that instructional support such as a toolbar with relevant elements and partly pre-drawn backgrounds improves drawing accuracy [N6-F2]. The “Can Drawing Help Students Learn Better?” Facebook post recommends asking learners to draw relationships rather than just objects, and to match assessment to the task [N7-R3]. This is important because it shifts the focus from mere object drawing to relational and task-aligned visual creation. The scaffolding evidence also supports low-stakes writing activities such as free writes, reflective paragraphs, peer response, and other exploratory tasks [N5-F3]. These are useful because they allow students to practice without fear of judgment, which is especially important for learners who may be reluctant to draw.

On how teachers can integrate drawing into writing instruction step-by-step, the evidence points to scaffolding, incremental support, and feedback loops. The scaffolding resource advises breaking writing assignments into smaller pieces, using low- and high-stakes activities, and providing feedback throughout the process [N5-F3]. It also recommends calculating how long students need to learn a specific task, inserting check-in points, and allowing revision with substantive reflection [N5-F3]. The ISLS paper similarly suggests that instructional support during drawing can reduce the cognitive load of the drawing task itself and improve accuracy [N6-F2]. A practical step-by-step approach would therefore involve: 1) introducing the task and providing a clear prompt or example; 2) offering low-stakes practice or brainstorming; 3) gradually increasing the complexity of the drawing task while providing support such as a drawing prompt, toolbar, or pre-drawn background; 4) giving feedback on the drawing and on underlying ideas; and 5) using the drawing as a basis for outlining, drafting, and revision [N5-F3][N6-F2][N7-R3]. The UAF survey also notes that illustrations can be used formatively to assess comprehension, which supports using drawing as a mid-process check rather than a final product [N4-F1].

On implementation barriers or resource needs, the evidence indicates that teachers need support materials, time for instruction, and feedback mechanisms. The ISLS paper states that the amount of instructional support needed is still an open question and that the study did not conduct a treatment-check of its drawing prompt [N6-F2]. This implies that teachers may need trial and adjustment rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. The scaffolding evidence also notes that complex writing tasks should be broken into smaller chunks and that teachers should build in low-stakes activities to encourage practice [N5-F3]. This suggests that implementation requires planning and sequencing rather than a single drawing activity. The UAF survey also highlights the need for prompts and examples to reduce reluctance to draw [N4-F1], which means teachers may need visual examples, templates, or shared examples to make drawing accessible. Finally, the scaffolding resource notes that students can receive feedback from teachers, classmates, consultants, and self-reflection [N5-F3], so implementation requires time and structures for feedback.

Overall, the evidence supports a practical implementation model in which drawing is introduced through prompts and examples, practiced in low-stakes settings, scaffolded into larger writing tasks, and supported by feedback and revision [N4-F1][N5-F3][N6-F2]. The main barriers are insufficient support, unclear prompts, and the need for time and feedback resources, while the main resource needs are instructional materials, examples, and feedback mechanisms [N4-F1][N5-F3][N6-F2].

## Integrated synthesis: how learner-generated drawings support story idea development and planning in writing tasks

Learner-generated drawings support writing tasks by helping students generate ideas, organize them, and then turn them into more coherent plans. The evidence from the branch reports suggests that drawing is not simply a decorative or artistic activity; it is a thinking tool that can help students externalize abstract ideas, make connections, and structure what they want to write. At the same time, the reports also show that drawing is most effective when it is supported by clear prompts, examples, and feedback, and when it is used as part of a broader scaffolding process. Below is a synthesis organized around the two main functions: idea development and planning.

---

## 1) How learner-generated drawings support story idea development

The branch report on idea development shows that drawing helps students visualize and expand story elements such as characters, settings, and plot points. The evidence is strongest on idea generation and brainstorming, with related claims about how drawing can support initial idea quantity, quality, or fluency.

### Visualizing and expanding story elements
The reports indicate that drawing can help students turn abstract ideas into concrete visual forms. The “Ideation: Brainstorming & Sketching” source describes a lesson that helps students refine ideas and “honing in on what form it will take, how it works, and why” [N1-R1]. The UAF Center for Teaching and Learning survey similarly notes that learner-generated drawing is similar to summarization, self-questioning, or prior knowledge activation, and that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience with creating illustrations [N4-F1]. This suggests that drawing can help students activate and expand story ideas by making them more concrete and visible.

The narrative and argumentative writing context strengthens this claim. The “Argumentative Essays” page states that argumentative writing requires students to investigate a topic, collect, generate, and evaluate evidence, and establish a position [N4-R5]. The “Inspiring Creative, Narrative, and Argumentative Writing with Art” video suggests that art can prompt students to write, which is consistent with the broader claim that visual creation can support narrative and argument development [N4-R2]. The UAF survey also says that examining student drawings can help instructors assess comprehension and identify possible shortcomings in understanding [N4-F1]. That is important because gaps in understanding can prevent coherent story ideas from emerging in the first place.

### Supporting connections between ideas and narrative/argument structure
The evidence also suggests that drawing supports connections between ideas. The UAF survey notes that learner-generated drawing can be used as a basis for learning activities and assessments, and that it can help learners represent subjects accurately [N4-F1]. The “comparing digital brainstorming tools in foreign language instruction” excerpt states that mind mapping reliably promotes idea generation, structural clarity, and task fluency [N1-R4]. Although that excerpt is not specifically about learner-generated drawings, it is still relevant because it shows that visual tools can improve structural clarity and fluency, which are essential for story development.

In the story-writing context, the idea is that drawing can help students move from isolated elements—such as characters, settings, and plot points—to a more connected narrative or argument. The UAF survey implies that drawing can support the emergence of structure by helping learners represent subjects accurately and by surfacing misunderstandings [N4-F1]. The “Argumentative Essays” page also emphasizes that argumentative writing requires generating and evaluating evidence, which is exactly the kind of idea connection that drawing can support by externalizing the evidence and the structure of the argument [N4-R5].

### Evidence of improvement in initial idea quantity, quality, or fluency
The evidence here is strongest for improvement in idea generation and fluency, rather than for a fully quantified writing-quality study. The “comparing digital brainstorming tools in foreign language instruction” excerpt states that mind mapping reliably promotes idea generation, structural clarity, and task fluency [N1-R4]. That is directly relevant because it shows that visual brainstorming tools can improve these outcomes, and drawing is a related visual strategy. The UAF survey also suggests that learners may need prompts and examples to reduce reluctance to draw, and that prompts can support the ideation process [N4-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports the claim that learner-generated drawings can improve initial idea quantity, quality, and fluency, especially when supported by prompts and examples [N1-R4][N4-F1].

---

## 2) How learner-generated drawings support planning and organizational thinking

The planning branch report shows that drawing helps students map out sequences, transitions, and logical flow, supports outlining, drafting, and revision decisions, and can contribute to more coherent writing products. The evidence here is more general than highly specific to writing tasks, but it still provides a solid foundation for explaining how drawing supports organizational thinking.

### Mapping sequences, transitions, and logical flow
The evidence indicates that drawing can help students structure their thinking and clarify what they are doing. The “Visual planning techniques” excerpt says that sketching helps people “structure things” and “clarify what I'm doing” [N2-R1]. The “adjusting organization for different types of writers” excerpt notes that some people need colors, cues, shapes, etc., on their planning page, while others want a hierarchy structure of ideas, which suggests that drawing can accommodate both visual and hierarchical ways of representing the order of a task [N2-R4]. This supports the claim that drawing can help students map sequences and transitions.

## Integrated synthesis: how learner-generated drawings support story idea development and planning in writing tasks

Learner-generated drawings support writing tasks by helping students generate ideas, organize them, and then turn them into more coherent plans. The evidence from the branch reports suggests that drawing is not simply a decorative or artistic activity; it is a thinking tool that can help students externalize abstract ideas, make connections, and structure what they want to write. At the same time, the reports also show that drawing is most effective when it is supported by clear prompts, examples, and feedback, and when it is used as part of a broader scaffolding process. Below is a synthesis organized around the two main functions: idea development and planning.

---

## 1) How learner-generated drawings support story idea development

The branch report on idea development shows that drawing helps students visualize and expand story elements such as characters, settings, and plot points. The evidence is strongest on idea generation and brainstorming, with related claims about how drawing can support initial idea quantity, quality, or fluency.

### Visualizing and expanding story elements
The reports indicate that drawing can help students turn abstract ideas into concrete visual forms. The UAF Center for Teaching and Learning survey similarly notes that learner-generated drawing is similar to summarization, self-questioning, or prior knowledge activation, and that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience with creating illustrations [N4-F1]. This suggests that drawing can help students activate and expand story ideas by making them more concrete and visible.

The narrative and argumentative writing context strengthens this claim. The “Argumentative Essays” page states that argumentative writing requires students to investigate a topic, collect, generate, and evaluate evidence, and establish a position [N4-R5]. The “Inspiring Creative, Narrative, and Argumentative Writing with Art” video suggests that art can prompt students to write, which is consistent with the broader claim that visual creation can support narrative and argument development [N4-R2]. The UAF survey also says that examining student drawings can help instructors assess comprehension and identify possible shortcomings in understanding [N4-F1]. That is important because gaps in understanding can prevent coherent story ideas from emerging in the first place.

### Supporting connections between ideas and narrative/argument structure
The evidence also suggests that drawing supports connections between ideas. The UAF survey notes that learner-generated drawing can be used as a basis for learning activities and assessments, and that it can help learners represent subjects accurately [N4-F1]. The “comparing digital brainstorming tools in foreign language instruction” excerpt states that mind mapping reliably promotes idea generation, structural clarity, and task fluency [N1-R4]. Although that excerpt is not specifically about learner-generated drawings, it is still relevant because it shows that visual tools can improve structural clarity and fluency, which are essential for story development.

In the story-writing context, the idea is that drawing can help students move from isolated elements—such as characters, settings, and plot points—to a more connected narrative or argument. The UAF survey implies that drawing can support the emergence of structure by helping learners represent subjects accurately and by surfacing misunderstandings [N4-F1]. The “Argumentative Essays” page also emphasizes that argumentative writing requires generating and evaluating evidence, which is exactly the kind of idea connection that drawing can support by externalizing the evidence and the structure of the argument [N4-R5].

### Evidence of improvement in initial idea quantity, quality, or fluency
The evidence here is strongest for improvement in idea generation and fluency, rather than for a fully quantified writing-quality study. The “comparing digital brainstorming tools in foreign language instruction” excerpt states that mind mapping reliably promotes idea generation, structural clarity, and task fluency [N1-R4]. That is directly relevant because it shows that visual brainstorming tools can improve these outcomes, and drawing is a related visual strategy. The UAF survey also suggests that learners may need prompts and examples to reduce reluctance to draw, and that prompts can support the ideation process [N4-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports the claim that learner-generated drawings can improve initial idea quantity, quality, and fluency, especially when supported by prompts and examples [N1-R4][N4-F1].

---

## 2) How learner-generated drawings support planning and organizational thinking

The planning branch report shows that drawing helps students map out sequences, transitions, and logical flow, supports outlining, drafting, and revision decisions, and can contribute to more coherent writing products. The evidence here is more general than highly specific to writing tasks, but it still provides a solid foundation for explaining how drawing supports organizational thinking.

### Mapping sequences, transitions, and logical flow
The evidence indicates that drawing can help students structure their thinking and clarify what they are doing. The “Visual planning techniques” excerpt says that sketching helps people “structure things” and “clarify what I'm doing” [N2-R1]. The “adjusting organization for different types of writers” excerpt notes that some people need colors, cues, shapes, etc., on their planning page, while others want a hierarchy structure of ideas, which suggests that drawing can accommodate both visual and hierarchical ways of representing the order of a task [N2-R4]. The evidence also supports outlining and revision. The YouTube example on creating an outline for persuasive writing shows that outlining is used to plan writing [N2-R2]. That is important for planning because it means drawing can reveal where students’ understanding is incomplete or fragmented, which can then be addressed before drafting begins.

The evidence for better planning or more coherent writing products is somewhat indirect, but still suggestive. The UAF survey says that learner-generated drawing is similar to summarization, self-questioning, or prior knowledge activation [N4-F1]. ## 3) Contextual factors and limitations

The contextual report shows that learner-generated drawings are not universally effective. Some learners and tasks benefit more, while others may not improve outcomes or may even be counterproductive if support is inadequate.

### Which learners and writing tasks benefit most
The evidence suggests that visual learners, students with little experience, and students needing scaffolding benefit most. The UAF survey notes that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience with creating illustrations [N4-F1]. The scaffolding evidence also emphasizes that novices often need support and that complex writing tasks should be broken into smaller chunks as students expand their skills [N5-F3]. The ISLS paper adds that benefits depend on drawing accuracy and that students need instructional support to draw accurately, with high-accuracy drawers outperforming low-accuracy drawers [N6-F2]. So the most beneficial population appears to be students who can produce accurate illustrations, which in turn depends on prior knowledge and instructional support.

The evidence is more cautionary here. The ISLS paper states that benefits strongly depend on drawing accuracy and that unsupported drawing does not automatically guarantee deep understanding [N6-F2]. The UAF survey also says that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience [N4-F1], which implies that unstructured drawing can be a barrier for some students. Taken together, the evidence suggests that drawing can interfere when students lack support, when the task becomes too cognitively demanding, or when students are asked to draw without clear guidance [N4-F1][N6-F2].

### How task design, instruction, and feedback affect effectiveness
The evidence strongly supports the idea that effective implementation depends on task design, instruction, and feedback. The ISLS paper explicitly says benefits depend on the amount of support required and that students need instructional support during the drawing process, including prompts and partly pre-drawn backgrounds [N6-F2]. The scaffolding evidence recommends breaking writing into smaller parts, using low- and high-stakes activities, providing feedback, and allowing revision [N5-F3]. It also emphasizes that instruction should gradually remove support as students become competent [N5-F3].

The UAF survey adds that prompts and examples can reduce reluctance to draw and that illustrations can be used formatively to assess comprehension [N4-F1]. These points indicate that effective implementation requires clear prompts, examples, feedback, and structured task design. The ISLS paper also notes that the amount of support needed is still an open question, and that the study did not conduct a treatment-check of its drawing prompt [N6-F2]. That means the evidence supports task design and instruction as crucial, but also acknowledges that the optimal amount of support is not fully settled [N6-F2].

---

## 4) Practical implementation and classroom use

The implementation report provides a concrete model for how teachers can use learner-generated drawing in writing lessons. It emphasizes well-designed activities, step-by-step integration, and attention to resource needs and barriers.

### Classroom activities or prompts that work best
The evidence suggests prompts, examples, and low-stakes practice work best. The UAF survey notes that learners may need prompts and examples, especially when they have little experience with creating illustrations [N4-F1]. The ISLS paper also emphasizes that instructional support such as a toolbar with relevant elements and partly pre-drawn backgrounds improves drawing accuracy [N6-F2]. This is important because it shifts the focus from mere object drawing to relational and task-aligned visual creation.

### How teachers can integrate drawing into writing instruction step-by-step
A practical step-by-step approach would involve:  
1) introducing the task and providing a clear prompt or example [N4-F1][N6-F2];  
2) offering low-stakes practice or brainstorming [N5-F3];  
3) gradually increasing the complexity of the drawing task while providing support such as a drawing prompt, toolbar, or pre-drawn background [N6-F2];  
4) giving feedback on the drawing and on underlying ideas [N5-F3][N4-F1];  
5) using the drawing as a basis for outlining, drafting, and revision [N5-F3][N7-R3].

The evidence indicates that teachers need support materials, time for instruction, and feedback mechanisms. The ISLS paper states that the amount of instructional support needed is still an open question and that the study did not conduct a treatment-check of its drawing prompt [N6-F2]. This implies that teachers may need trial and adjustment rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. The scaffolding evidence also notes that complex writing tasks should be broken into smaller chunks and that teachers should build in low-stakes activities to encourage practice [N5-F3]. This suggests that implementation requires planning and sequencing rather than a single drawing activity. The UAF survey also highlights the need for prompts and examples to reduce reluctance to draw [N4-F1], which means teachers may need visual examples, templates, or shared examples to make drawing accessible. Finally, the scaffolding resource notes that students can receive feedback from teachers, classmates, consultants, and self-reflection [N5-F3], so implementation requires time and structures for feedback.

---

## 5) Overall conclusion

Learner-generated drawings support story idea development and planning in writing tasks in several ways. First, they help students visualize and expand story elements such as characters, settings, and plot points [N1-R1][N4-F1]. Second, they support connections between ideas and the emergence of narrative or argument structure [N4-F1][N4-R5]. Third, they can improve initial idea quantity, quality, and fluency, especially when supported by prompts and examples [N1-R4][N4-F1]. However, the evidence also shows that drawing is most effective for certain learners and tasks and may not improve outcomes if support is inadequate, the task becomes too cognitively demanding, or the drawing process is not well scaffolded [N4-F1][N6-F2]. Practical implementation depends on clear prompts, examples, feedback, and structured task design [N4-F1][N5-F3][N6-F2].

In short: learner-generated drawing is not simply about art; it is a thinking tool that can help students generate ideas, organize them, and plan writing more effectively, but only when it is supported by instruction, feedback, and task design.
